query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of silicon (Si) as a dopant into the boride-based alloy will improve the resistance to molten‐aluminum corrosion by promoting the in situ formation of a continuous, Si‐rich intermetallic barrier at the alloy surface during service.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components as currently manufactured for hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, having the standard undoped boride microstructure and phase distribution.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by adding roughly 2–5 at.% silicon during processing to produce a silicon-doped boride alloy via the same melting/casting route used for the baseline.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum under typical hot-dip plating conditions (e.g., ~660 °C) for durations representative of industrial service; the intervention should remain effective provided the Si content stays within the targeted range and the thermal profile does not deviate significantly from standard operating temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, continuous Si-rich intermetallic or silicide layer at the alloy surface upon exposure to molten aluminum, which serves as a diffusion barrier and limits interfacial attack.
generation.mechanism: Si segregates during high-temperature exposure and reacts with the boride matrix to form a stable, adherent Si-rich barrier layer. This layer decreases molten aluminum wettability and retards dissolution or penetration of the underlying boride phases, thereby reducing corrosion kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to undoped boride components, the Si-doped variant is expected to exhibit a significant reduction in corrosion rate (e.g., an approximate 30–50% decrease in penetration depth or weight loss over the same exposure time) when immersed in molten aluminum at plating temperatures.
generation.baseline: Standard boride-based components without Si doping, which are known to experience measurable molten-aluminum corrosion under hot-dip plating conditions.
generation.boundary: The improved corrosion resistance is expected to hold under typical hot-dip aluminum plating conditions (~660 °C) and with Si levels maintained in the range of 2–5 at.%; degradation of the barrier may occur if the Si content is too low to form a continuous layer or if operating temperatures vary widely from the norm.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum Si concentration and the exact magnitude of improvement remain uncertain without preliminary alloy screening. In addition, the kinetics of barrier formation and its long-term stability under cyclic thermal exposures require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based specimens: one set with the Si-doping (2–5 at.%) and one set as the undoped baseline. Expose both sets to molten aluminum at ~660 °C in a controlled crucible test mimicking hot-dip plating conditions for a fixed time (e.g., 100 hours). After exposure, perform cross-sectional metallography, SEM/EDX analysis for interfacial layer identification, and weight loss or corrosion-penetration measurements.
measurements: Corrosion depth (penetration distance) measured by metallography
Weight loss of specimens after exposure
Characterization of the interfacial layer (phase, continuity, composition) using SEM/EDX
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-doped specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., less than a 30% improvement) in corrosion depth or weight loss compared to the undoped baseline, or if no continuous Si-rich barrier layer is observed on the Si-doped specimens, then the hypothesis is falsified.
